title: Design Bitset
statement:
Design a class `Bitset` that holds a fixed row of bits, numbered from `0`, and supports these calls:

- `Bitset(size)` creates `size` bits, every one set to `0`.
- `fix(idx)` makes bit `idx` equal to `1` (nothing changes if it already is).
- `unfix(idx)` makes bit `idx` equal to `0` (nothing changes if it already is).
- `flip()` inverts every bit: each `0` turns into `1` and each `1` into `0`.
- `all()` returns `true` exactly when every bit is `1`.
- `one()` returns `true` exactly when at least one bit is `1`.
- `count()` returns how many bits are `1`.
- `toString()` returns a string of `size` characters `'0'`/`'1'` whose character at position `i` is bit `i`.
constraints: At most 10^5 calls in total are made to fix, unfix, flip, all, one, count and toString
At least one call is made to all, one, count or toString
At most 5 calls are made to toString
notes:
## Intuition

The direct way stores every bit and, on `flip()`, walks the whole row, which is O(size) per flip. Flipping twice changes nothing, so instead of touching every bit we keep one flag that says whether the row is currently inverted. A stored bit's real value is then `bits[i] ^ flipped`. Keeping a running count of ones makes `count`, `all` and `one` instant, and a flip simply turns `ones` into `size - ones`.

## Approach

1. Store `size`, an array `bits` of zeros, a flag `flipped = 0` and a counter `ones = 0`.
2. `fix(idx)`: if the real bit `bits[idx] ^ flipped` is 0, toggle the stored bit and add one to `ones`.
3. `unfix(idx)`: if the real bit is 1, toggle the stored bit and subtract one from `ones`.
4. `flip()`: toggle `flipped` and set `ones = size - ones`.
5. `all()`, `one()` and `count()` compare or return `ones`.
6. `toString()`: XOR every stored bit with `flipped` and join them; it runs at most 5 times.

## Example 1, step by step

`Bitset(5)` gives `bits = [0,0,0,0,0]`. `fix(3)` and `fix(1)` set those stored bits, so `ones = 2`. `flip()` sets `flipped = 1` and `ones = 3` (real row `10101`); `all()` is `false`. `unfix(0)`: the real bit is `0 ^ 1 = 1`, so stored bit 0 becomes 1 and `ones = 2`. `flip()` sets `flipped = 0` and `ones = 3` (real row `11010`); `one()` is `true`. `unfix(0)` clears stored bit 0, `ones = 2`, so `count()` returns `2` and `toString()` returns `"01010"`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(1) for every call except `toString`, which is O(size).
- Space: O(size) for the stored bits.

## Pitfalls

- `fix` and `unfix` must check the real value first; changing `ones` when the bit already has the wanted value double counts.
- After a flip the stored array no longer equals the real row, so always read through `^ flipped`.
- Do not rebuild the string on every update; it is only needed in `toString`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `size` | number of bits |
| `bits` | stored bits before the pending inversion is applied |
| `flipped` | 1 when the whole row is currently inverted, else 0 |
| `ones` | how many real bits are 1 |
